Price, Shirley Lee (Edwards) · Prime 4 A life · 1925–1995 · Neodesha, Kansas

Shirley Lee Edwards Price
A Neodesha Life

↑² MF— paternal grandmother of Brent (the anchor of this page)Proven

Shirley Edwards was a Neodesha girl — daughter of Ira P. Edwards and Ruth T. Jones Edwards — who quit school in her senior year, rode to Texas, and married a paratrooper at nine o'clock on a Saturday night in August 1942. She was seventeen. The husband was Kenneth Fred Price, whose own story is told on his page; this one is hers.

She outlived him by thirty-five years. Widowed at thirty-five with two children, she learned the butcher's trade from nothing when his pension got tangled in a wound the Army had coded “not in line of duty,” worked until a fall put her on disability, cared for her mother to the end of Ruth's life — and fought the Veterans Administration over that pension for the rest of her own. She never left Neodesha. This page tells her whole life, grades every claim it makes, and leaves the open questions open.

§1 The woman

The records know her under one name in three forms: Shirley Edwards in the hometown paper, Shirley L. Price in the indexes, and Shirley Lee Edwards Price in the family's keeping. The middle name is the soft spot — it rides on family usage and tree data, and no vital record in the file has yet shown it. Everything else about who she was is harder than that.

She was the daughter of Ira P. Edwards and Ruth T. (Jones) Edwards of Neodesha, Wilson County, Kansas — the wedding announcement of August 1942 calls her, in print, “daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Ira Edwards,” and her mother's 1993 obituary names the same couple from the other end of their lives. Proven Her younger sister was Dorene “Dodie” Edwards, later of Tulsa — the family's other witness, whose 2009 letter carries half of what this page knows about Shirley's character. Proven

She married once, at seventeen, and the marriage lasted eighteen years, until death ended it. She had two children: Sharon Lou, born 9 December 1944, and Kenneth Lee, born 1946 — the son this page's family descends through. Proven · family record

Two people who knew her best described her, independently, in letters written two days apart in January 2009, and their accounts agree in substance: quiet, reserved, kind past the point of sense, and stubborn about never asking for help. Those letters — her sister Dorene's and her daughter Sherry's — are quoted in this page at the places where the records run out. They are family testimony, and the page grades them that way: Probable, never proof. Where a claim on this page rests on one of them, the chip says so.

The shape of the evidence. Shirley's life is documented at its hinges — a wedding announcement, one census sheet, an obituary index row, a cemetery deed, a headstone — and remembered in between. The hinges are iron. The in-between is two women's letters and a paper trail of addresses. This page keeps the two kinds separate, claim by claim.

§2 The census trail

Four canvases should hold her: the Kansas state census of 1925, taken two months before she was born, and the federal censuses of 1930, 1940 and 1950. Only one of the four has been read. The trail is told here as it stands — one sheet in hand, three instruments still waiting — because the unread sheets are exactly where her open questions live.

1925 — Kansas state censusThe birthplace instrument · unread

Kansas counted its people on 1 March 1925, ten weeks before Shirley was born. The sheet for Ira and Ruth Edwards — married the April before in Indianapolis — would show where the couple was living that spring: Indianapolis still, or Neodesha already. That one line would not be her birth record, but it would weigh the birthplace question harder than anything else short of one. The Wilson County index sits behind a login wall and on microfilm; the read has not been made. Open

1930 — United States censusRoute pinned · sheet unread

She would be four, turning five, in her father's house — the first federal sheet that can name her. A 1930 census record is attached as a source to her FamilySearch page, but the sheet itself has never been read in this research: the free route is a manual one, the Internet Archive's copy of the fifteenth census, Wilson County enumeration districts 103-1 through 103-28, over a thousand images with no usable text layer. Until someone walks those images, her childhood household — its street, its neighbors, her father's stated work — is unread, not unknown. Open

1940 — United States censusAttached as a source · sheet unread

She would be fourteen, in the Neodesha schools the wedding notice names, two years from the marriage that ends the Edwards chapter of her life. A 1940 record likewise rides her tree page as an attached source; the image has not been read here either. The 1940 sheet carries one thing no later record can: the household as it stood on the edge of the war, before her father's classroom changed it. Open

1950 — United States censusED 103-18 · sheet 12 · read in full

The one sheet in hand, and it is a good one. On 10 April 1950 the enumerator found the family at 213 South 5th Street, Neodesha: Kenneth, 28, working forty hours a week as a burner at the Independent Plant; Shirley, 24, keeping house; Sharon, 5; and Kenneth Lee, 3. It is the only census that catches the marriage whole — husband, wife, both children, one roof — and it fixes the address that the rest of her story keeps returning to. Proven

After 1950 the federal trail ends, as it does for everyone; the census goes quiet for seventy-two years at a time. Her widowhood is traced instead through the address records in §11 — thinner paper, but it holds two street addresses and thirty-five years of staying in one town.

§3 A Sunday in May

Her parents married on 8 April 1924 in Indianapolis, Indiana: Ira P. Edwards and Ruth T. Jones, twenty-eight, born 28 July 1905 in Humansville, Missouri, the daughter of Bertram and Dora Mae Blaker Jones. Proven · Ruth's obituary

Thirteen months later, on Sunday, 10 May 1925, Shirley was born. The date is not in doubt: it is cut into her headstone — SHIRLEY L. PRICE / MAY 10 1925 | JUNE 19 1995 — and the Social Security death entry agrees with the stone to the day. Proven · headstone

Where she was born, no record in hand says. The paper trail leans one way: she arrived thirteen months after a wedding in Indianapolis, and new couples do not always move fast. The hometown paper leans the other: the 1942 wedding notice says she had “lived in Neodesha most of her life” — and most, not all, leaves the door open exactly where Indianapolis stands. No birth announcement has been found in either town's papers. This page asserts a date and declines to assert a place. Birthplace: open

The stone outranks the databases. Ancestry long carried her born 1 May 1925 and died 9 June 1995; her FamilySearch page carried the same wrong pair until it was corrected on 4 October 2026. Both alternates are disproven by the marker itself, photographed and transcribed: 10 May 1925 – 19 June 1995. Where a database and a headstone disagree, this page follows the stone. Alternates disproved

§4 The quiet girl

By the time any record can see her, she was a Neodesha girl: the 1942 notice says she had lived in Neodesha most of her life and received her education in the Neodesha schools — so the Edwards family settled in Wilson County while she was still small, sometime in the late 1920s. The street they lived on is one of the unread census sheets' secrets. Town proven · street open

What she was like comes from her sister. Dorene remembered her growing up quiet and reserved — Dorene “made enough trouble and noise for both of us,” and never understood how they had the same parents. Shirley was never social-minded, never went to dances — “until she met Kenneth during the war.” Probable · sister's testimony

“Growing up she was quiet and reserved — I made enough trouble and noise for both of us… She was never social minded, never went to dances, Etc., until she met Kenneth during the war.”

— Dorene “Dodie” Edwards Hull, email to Brent Price, 4 January 2009

She had one gift nobody formalized: a special knack for design, a real talent for clothes. Dorene believed she could have been a promising clothes designer, and wished some pictures of her designs had survived. None have surfaced — the talent is attested, the work is gone, and the page records both halves of that sentence. Probable · no designs survive

§5 Her father's classroom

The war brought him to her. Her father Ira was teaching a class — “something to do with machines for the war effort” — and Kenneth Price was in it: twenty years old, an Army private out of Fort Leavenworth, headed for the parachute battalion at Camp Wolters in Texas.

That is Dorene's telling, and it is the only telling there is — no class roster or training record has surfaced to stand beside it. It is kept here as what it is: family testimony from the sister who was there, graded accordingly, and not promoted into record. Probable · family testimony

She was sixteen, seventeen — a senior in the Neodesha schools, the quiet girl who never went to dances. Dorene's account of what happened next is spare and direct: Shirley met Kenneth during the war, quit school in her senior year, and “went to Palo Texas and got married.” The diploma and the design talent went together — unfinished, unpictured, carried into the marriage instead. Probable · sister's testimony

§6 Palo Pinto, nine o'clock

They married at nine o'clock on Saturday night, 1 August 1942, at Palo Pinto, Texas — the Neodesha paper spelled it “Polo Pinto,” twice, in its own hand — the Rev. Walker, pastor of the Christian church there, reading the vows. She was seventeen. He was a private in the parachute battalion at Camp Wolters, forty miles of Texas away. It was a scorching north-Texas Saturday: 99 degrees at the top of the afternoon, 76 overnight, not a drop of rain. Proven · the announcement Weather: NOAA approximation

The announcement ran in The Neodesha News on 6 August 1942. It is reproduced here in full, because it is the load-bearing document of her early life: it proves her parentage, her marriage, her schooling — and it is the earliest family document that names Kenneth a paratrooper.

Edwards – Price.

Miss Shirley Edwards, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Ira Edwards, and Pvt. Kenneth F. Price, of Pittsburg, Kan., were married at 9:00 p. m. Saturday, August 1, at Polo Pinto, Texas. Rev. Walker, pastor of the Christian church at Polo Pinto read the marriage vows.

Pvt. Price is a member of the parachute battalion and is stationed at Camp Wolters, Texas. They will establish their home at Mineral Wells, for the present.

Mrs. Price has lived in Neodesha most of her life and received her education in the Neodesha schools. Pvt. Price, while not so well-known here, has visited here on numerous occasions and made many friends, who join those of his bride in extending congratulations and best wishes.

Read it closely and it gives up four facts and one plan. The facts: her parents' names; the marriage, its hour and its officiant; her Neodesha schooling. The plan: “They will establish their home at Mineral Wells, for the present.” Whether they ever kept that home, no record shows — the paper recorded the intention, not the occupancy, and the file keeps the two apart. Mineral Wells: unproved One line cuts the other way across the state line: the paper calls the groom “of Pittsburg, Kan.,” while the Price family's own records put his people in Labette County. That quarrel belongs to his page; it is flagged here so it is flagged everywhere. Cross-line conflict, kept visible

§7 The war years — her side of his war

By the spring of 1943 she was back in Neodesha, and the paper proves it: on 15 April 1943 the Neodesha News reported that “T. Sgt. Kenneth Price … is spending a three weeks furlough in Neodesha with his wife” — a brand-new technical sergeant, home from the staging pipeline, three weeks with his seventeen-year-old wife. Proven · Neodesha News

The photographs on this page belong to this season of their lives. None of them carries a date; the family places them in the marriage season of 1942, around the wedding and the furloughs, and the page keeps that placing at the grade it deserves. Family placing

The war took him from there: England by June 1943, Sicily in July. On his first jump he was shot out of the sky, and the Army's hospital admission card — found in October 2026, and set out in full on his page — records the wound exactly: a rifle bullet through the index and middle fingers, amputation, the loss of part of his left hand. He came home in December 1943, discharged for disability. Proven · hospital card

What the card also did — the coding that would run the rest of Shirley's life — belongs to §10. Here it is enough to mark the fact: the same card coded that combat wound “not in line of duty,” and the discharge “not in line of duty (existed prior to service).” The hometown paper, that same season, wrote of “wounds received in the invasion of Sicily.” Both documents exist. Shirley spent thirty-five years living in the gap between them. The coding stands unresolved

After Ken came back from overseas, Dorene remembered, they came back to Neodesha. For good. Probable · sister's testimony

§8 213 South 5th

They made Neodesha home for good. Sharon Lou was born in Neodesha Township on 9 December 1944; Kenneth Lee followed in 1946 — the two children of the marriage, the “new kids” of Dorene's telling. Proven · family record

The 1950 census found them at 213 South 5th Street — Kenneth burning at the Independent Plant, Shirley keeping house, the children five and three. The hometown paper still caught the family whole in March 1951: “Mrs. Kenneth Price, Mr. Price and children, Sharon and Kenny,” at the 55th anniversary of Shirley's grandparents, the N. C. Edwardses. The paper, March 1951

Sherry — Sharon Lou, the daughter — remembered that house as the warm center of the neighborhood. They didn't have money, she wrote, but she never knew it growing up: she and Ken always had birthday parties, and every kid in the class was invited, because their mother said no child would have hurt feelings by not being invited. In her teens Sherry would come home from a date to find one of her friends crying on her mother's shoulder about a boyfriend — they came to Shirley instead of their own mothers. Slumber parties every few weeks, sixteen girls at a time; formals for the school dances and the Job's Daughters dances; every holiday gone all-out with decorations and special cookies; Christmas trees cut in the woods until Ken's cedar allergy forced store-bought pines.

“I know life had to be full of money worries but Ken and I never knew it until we were old enough to understand.”

— Sharon “Sherry” Price Myers, email to Brent Price, 7 January 2009

Kenneth's work shifted over the decade; by his death he was at the Continental Can Company in Coffeyville — his obituary says so, and the family memorial calls him a machinist there: the machine-shop trade the Army had noted in 1942, carried through the war and home again. No plant record has surfaced, so the detail stands on those two voices. Probable · two voices

And then, in September 1960, Kenneth died — in his sleep, at home, sometime after 2 a.m. on Friday, 2 September, of a heart attack, in the same house the census had counted a decade before. He was thirty-nine. His obituary names the survivors plainly: “the wife, Mrs. Shirley Price; a son, Kenneth, and a daughter, Sharon, all of the home.” When the VA headstone application was made, it was Shirley who furnished the address — 213 South 5th Street, the widow at the house that was still hers. Proven · his obituary

She was thirty-five years old, with a daughter of fifteen and a son of fourteen, and a pension already tangled in a coding she did not yet know she would fight for the rest of her life.

§9 The butcher shop

This is the chapter Dorene wrote, and the family has always told. When Kenneth's pension and stuff got all fouled up — the wound coded “not in line of duty” — Shirley went to work. She had never worked a day in her life, and now she had to, to raise those kids.

“Shirley had never worked a day in her life but when Ken's pension and stuff got all fouled up she had to, to raise those new kids. She went to work as a butcher in a local grocery — she didn't know one end of a pig from another but she learned and was good.”

— Dorene “Dodie” Edwards Hull, 4 January 2009

The store's name, the years she worked, the pay: none of it is in the file. The butcher years are real on her sister's word and empty on paper — the only stretch of her working life, and no record of it has been found. It stands in the ledger at the grade the evidence earns. Probable · the store is unnamed

One day she fell at work, and had to go on disability. After that she more or less looked after her mother. Ruth lived on into her late eighties; when she aged and needed care, Shirley moved her into her own small apartment, and when Ruth needed more care than that, Shirley sat in the nursing home in her mother's room all day, every day — Sherry took Saturdays and Dodie took Sundays so she could get some rest. Ruth died at the Golden Keys Nursing Home in Neodesha on 2 November 1993, and her obituary names the daughters among the survivors: “Shirley Price of Neodesha” and “Dorene A. Hull of Tulsa.” Proven · Ruth's obituary

Sherry filled in what that looking-after looked like from the inside: rides given to people, to doctors' offices and grocery stores; errands run for anyone who asked. “There was nothing she would not do for others. She was kind to everyone.” She remembered arguing with her mother over clothes — Shirley buying for her daughter while wearing the same red coat for as long as Sherry could remember.

She was never well, Dorene wrote — she inherited both her mother and dad's heart conditions, and the doctors were never able to figure out what was wrong with her. But the same voice that says that says this: “She was the best mother to her kids and when times were lean she would do without things for herself to make sure those kids had what they needed. And do you think she would ask for help — no way.” There were good days in the telling too: when the family came to Claremore to see Sherry and her family, they'd come over to Dorene's the next day, and Dorene would take a day off, and they'd go to the mall together. “She loved this.” Probable · sister's testimony

The center chapter

The fight

A rifle bullet took part of her husband's left hand in Sicily. The Army's card called it “not in line of duty.” Shirley Price spent the rest of her life telling the government it was wrong.

Status: the coding stands unreconciled · the claims file that documents her fight is still outstanding

Start with the two documents, because the whole fight lives between them. The first is the Army's hospital admission card for Kenneth F. Price, serial 17057680, pulled from the Surgeon General's files in October 2026: admitted July 1943 in North Africa; diagnosis, a penetrating wound of the index and middle fingers; causative agent, bullet, rifle; treatment, amputation; final result, loss of part of the left hand. And in the line-of-duty field, the words: “Not in line of duty: misconduct and all others.” His discharge, that December, reads the same way: discharged for disability, not in line of duty (existed prior to service). Proven · the card, transcribed

The second document is the hometown paper, which wrote of Kenneth's “wounds received in the invasion of Sicily” — a paratrooper of the 82nd Airborne's Sicily summer, shot on his first jump, in the telling his own page weighs in full. A wound received jumping into Sicily is, on its face, a wound in the line of duty. The card says otherwise, in the flat language of a punch-card clerk, and the card is what the Veterans Administration paid on. The conflict is unresolved

The family's account of the tangle goes further, and this page reports it as the family's account, not as record: that Kenneth's service papers were sunk coming home from the war, and that the records of two men named Kenneth Price were crossed and never fully fixed. What the documents in hand prove is narrower and bad enough — a combat wound carrying a coding that reads like a clerical verdict against the man who took it, and a widow left to argue with it. Family account · unproven in its details

So she argued. The family's story, told plainly, is that Shirley fought the VA over Kenneth's pension for the rest of her life and never received it in full. The claims and appeals themselves — the letters, the decisions, the years of them — live in one file: Kenneth's VA claims file, the C-file, which would document her fight year by year in the government's own hand. It has been requested. It is not in hand. Brent sends that request himself, and until it lands, the fight is the best-attested unwritten chapter in either of their stories: everyone who knew her testifies to it, and no page of it can yet be quoted. VA claims file: outstanding

What her side of the story adds to his. On Kenneth's page, the “not in line of duty” coding is an open question in a records hunt — the morning reports are named as its judge. On this page it is something else: the reason a woman who had never worked a day in her life was cutting meat in a grocery in her late thirties, and the opponent she faced, alone, for thirty-five years. The same two documents; two different weights. Both pages carry the question open, because neither has the file that closes it.

§11 Thirty-five years a widow

She never left Neodesha. The widowhood is the longest chapter of her life and the thinnest in paper — no census will ever count it — but the address records, read closely, trace a woman staying put in one small town for thirty-five years.

In November 1965 she bought her own burial ground: the Neodesha Cemetery listing shows the family lot — 1st Addition, Block 6, Lot 975 — with her mother Ruth in space 2, Shirley in space 3 under a deed dated 11 November 1965, and Kenneth in space 4. She was forty years old, five years a widow, arranging the row she would lie in for the next thirty. Proven · cemetery listing

Her street addresses for those years come from the public-records indexes, and they answer the question the research had carried as its biggest residence gap. The U.S. Public Records Index (Volume 1, record 352014237) holds Shirley L. Price, born 10 May 1925, at 213 S. 5th Street — the 1950 house, still hers in the index — and at a second address, 214 N. 7th Street, Neodesha. The FamilySearch public-records collection carries her in Neodesha into the 1990s as well. Index entries are not deeds; they are captures, not tenancies, and their dates run sloppy — one entry trails to 2001, six years past her death, the way directory paper always lags. The streets themselves are what the index is good for, and the streets are these two. Index grade · read 17 Oct 2026

One address claim does not survive the same reading: the family tree long carried a residence for her at Independence, Kansas, in 1996 — dated a year after she died. No source places her in Independence at any date; the entry reads as directory lag or a misattached citation, and it is carried in the ledger as disproved as stated. Disproved as stated

Her greatest joy, Sherry wrote, came when she became a grandmother. She talked about Brandon and Brent all the time, and loved to come see her daughter's kids. The quiet girl of §4 ended as the woman two generations gathered around — the mother her children's friends cried to, the grandmother whose name the boys carried back to her. Probable · daughter's testimony

She died on Monday, 19 June 1995, aged seventy, in Neodesha. Her obituary ran in the Neodesha Daily on Thursday, 22 June 1995, page 3 — the Wilson County Master Obituary Index preserves the row exactly: Price | Shirley L (EDWARDS) | Neodesha | ND | 22-Jun-1995 | 3 | Age: 70, with the death-date column left blank, as if the index itself were waiting on the same document this page is waiting on. The full obituary text — which would pin her birthplace, her funeral, her survivors in her own town's words — has been requested from the W. A. Rankin Memorial Library, first on 3 October 2026 and again by follow-up on 16 October 2026. No reply has come. It remains the single most valuable missing document in her file. Obituary: requested, not received

She is buried where she arranged to be. Brent was at her funeral — his testimony is firsthand and closes the question the cemetery listing left blank: “She's there. I went to her funeral.” Her Find a Grave memorial, 84656585, carries the stone's dates; the memorial numbered 145841439, a “Shirley A. Price, 1949–1995,” is a different woman and must never be merged with her. Proven · firsthand testimony

§12 The proof trail

Her open questions are not mysteries; they are unmailed letters and unread sheets. Every one of them has a named instrument, and most of the instruments are already in motion.

The one letter

Her obituary — Neodesha Daily, 22 June 1995, page 3 — is a single library reply away. The W. A. Rankin Memorial Library in Neodesha holds the paper; the lookup was requested on 3 October 2026, and a follow-up went out on 16 October 2026. A hometown obituary of that era typically gives the birthplace, the funeral home, the burial, and the survivors in five column inches: it would close or sharpen at least four of this page's open items at once, including the birthplace question that has stood since the research began. Nothing else on this page is one envelope from resolution. The reply, when it comes, folds into this page the same round it lands.

§13 The verdict ledger

Every material proposition in her file, with its standing. Filter by standing to see how much of the story is bedrock, how much is family's word, and how much is still open.

OpenHer birthplace — Indianapolis (her parents married there thirteen months before she was born) against Neodesha (the paper's “most of her life” — most, not all). No birth record has been pulled; no birth announcement found in either town.
OpenThe 1925 Kansas state census and the 1930 and 1940 federal sheets for Ira's household — where they lived, on what street, with which neighbors. Routes are pinned; the reads have not been made.
OpenWhether the couple ever kept the Mineral Wells home the announcement promised “for the present” — the paper records the plan, not the occupancy.
OpenThe grocery where she worked as a butcher — its name, her years there, and any record of the fall that ended her working life.
OpenThe occasion of the hand-colored embrace — the family's placing is the marriage season of 1942; the print itself carries no date.
OpenHer full obituary (Neodesha Daily, 22 June 1995, p. 3) — requested from the W. A. Rankin Memorial Library 3 October 2026, followed up 16 October 2026; no reply yet.
OpenKenneth's VA claims file — the paper record of her decades of claims and appeals over his pension. Requested; Brent sends it himself; not in hand.
OpenA cross-line conflict, kept visible rather than settled here: her husband's birth year — 1917 on his headstone and cemetery listing, about 1921–22 in the censuses, his draft card, and his obituary. It is weighed on his page; her page does not borrow a verdict.

§14 Open questions

  1. The full obituary. Neodesha Daily, 22 June 1995, page 3 — birthplace, funeral details, survivors, and likely her last address, in five column inches. Requested from the W. A. Rankin Memorial Library on 3 October 2026; follow-up sent 16 October 2026; no reply on file. It is the file's single most valuable missing document.
  2. The VA claims file. Her decades of claims and appeals over Kenneth's pension — the documentary record of §10's fight. Brent sends the request himself; the file has not arrived, and no page of it can be quoted until it does.
  3. Birthplace. Indianapolis against Neodesha. The instruments, in order: the obituary; the 1925 Kansas state census, which shows where Ira and Ruth were living ten weeks before she was born; the Kansas death certificate, a paid record that is the family's call.
  4. The unread census sheets. 1925 (Kansas), 1930 and 1940 (federal) — her childhood household and street. The 1930 route is pinned to the Internet Archive's Wilson County districts; the 1940 sheet rides her FamilySearch page as an attached source, its image unread here.
  5. The grocery. The name of the store where she worked as a butcher, her years there, and any record of the fall. City directories and the full obituary are the likeliest namers.
  6. Mineral Wells, 1942. Plan against occupancy: whether the couple ever kept the Texas home the announcement promised. Kenneth's Camp Wolters morning reports are the only known route.
  7. The hand-colored embrace. Which occasion — wedding leave, a furlough, an ordinary afternoon — the family's most-loved photograph of them actually marks. A family question, carried open on the caption itself.
  8. A family memoir. A separate written remembrance of Shirley circulates in the family's papers; its authorship is unverified, and by the family's standing ruling it stays personal, in the family's hands. The two attributed letters — Dorene's and Sherry's, both January 2009 — are the testimony this page quotes.
